To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a set of genes, which were over-expressing in the primary tumor of the breast cancer patients, were also over-expressing after chemotherapy in the good responders and in the bad responders.
a set of genes, over-expressed in post chemotherapy breast cancer cells, may be considered as key molecules driving breast cancer chemoresistances.

(i) a significant number of genes were over-expressing after neoadjuvant treatment in all histopathological groups; (ii) a set of genes were overexpressing only in the good and the bad response group; (iii) a subset of these genes were up-regulated only in the good response group.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to breast cancer therapy based on the identification of key molecular pathways driving chemoresistance, which may be used to develop novel therapeutic strategies.
identifying the molecular mechanisms underlying chemoresistance in breast cancer and with the identification of potential targets for future therapies.
the identification of molecular mechanisms which are responsible for breast cancer chemoresistant phenotype.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the present study, we identified a transcriptional shift that occurs during breast cancer chemoresistant cell selection, identifying a set of key genes that may become appropriate targets to develop novel drugs for breast cancer treatment.
, in the present study, we identified a set of genes which, in a significant proportion of patients, are overexpressed after chemotherapy.
the molecular pathways identified in this work may be used to identify a set of genes driving breast cancer chemoresistence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have identified a set of genes that can be used as markers of the chemoresistance in the breast cancer and that these genes are involved in the cell cycle regulation, cell adhesion and cell migration.
we found that the genes which drive breast cancer chemo-resistance are not the same as the genes which drive primary tumor growth.

the molecular mechanisms which drive breast cancer cells to become resistant to anthracyclines and taxanes, the most common chemotherapeutic agents, are not only the same, but they are also the same which are responsible for the survival of the tumor in its natural environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in breast cancer, the transcriptional profile of the primary tumor is not predictive of the response to neoadjuvant treatment.
a transcriptional shift occurs in breast cancer cells following anthracycline- and taxane-based neoadjuvant treatment, which identifies a set of genes driving the chemoresistant phenotype.

, in order to identify key molecular targets, it is important to analyze the expression profile of the same tumor both before and after the administration of the drug, and to consider the histological response of the tumor to the drug.
